extracted.intended_audience: naturalists, geographers, and educated readers interested in climatology, plant geography, and meteorology
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition of principles, measurements, and empirical rules governing climate, atmospheric moisture and electricity, snow-line, and their influence on plant distribution and cultivation (19th-century physical geography).

rubrics_metrics.name: Plant cultivation depends on multiple climatic relations
rubrics_metrics.description: If we ... begin with those plants which require the hottest climate ... an exact geographical consideration of the limits of cultivation ... will teach us that other climatic relations besides those of mean annual temperature are involved in these phenomena.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples given (vanilla, cacao, banana, pine-apples, sugar-cane, coffee, dates, cotton, citrons, olives, chestnuts, vines) illustrate that mean annual temperature alone is insufficient to predict cultivation limits; other factors (seasonal distribution of heat, light intensity, humidity, exposure, elevation, local configuration) must be considered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vine (potable wine) temperature requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: In order to procure 'potable' wine it is requisite that the mean annual heat should exceed 49 degrees, that the winter temperature upward of 64 degrees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The statement is illustrated by a table of observational examples (Bordeaux, Potsdam, Rhine, Maine, Cherbourg, Dublin) showing how similar mean thermometer readings can still yield different vine ripeness depending on cloudiness and sunshine; author emphasizes that thermometers in shade do not capture surface insolation effects that affect vine ripeness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thermometer-in-shade caveat: shade thermometers do not equal surface temperature
rubrics_metrics.description: A thermometer standing in the shade, and protected from the effect of direct insolation and nocturnal radiation can not, at all seasons of the year, and during all periodic changes of heat, indicate the true superficial temperature of the ground exposed to the whole effect of the sun's rays.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use caution when using standard shaded thermometers to infer plant-surface temperatures or ripening conditions; refer to Dove's 15 years observations at Chiswick Gardens for inferred differences between shaded air temperature and true surface temperature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Isothermal system principle: three-element connection
rubrics_metrics.description: In each system of 'isothermal' lines of equal curvature there reigns a close and necessary connection between three elements, namely, the decrease of heat in a vertical direction from below upward, the difference of temperature for every one degree of geographical latitude, and the uniformity in the mean temperature of a mountain station, and the latitude of a point situated at the level of the sea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This principle links lapse-rate, latitudinal gradient, and equivalence of mountain elevation to sea-level latitude; use it to compare climates of mountain stations to climates at different latitudes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Central Europe numerical relations: latitudinal and vertical temperature gradients
rubrics_metrics.description: Between the parallels of 38 degrees and 71 degrees I found that the decrease of temperature was very regularly 0.9 degrees for every degree of latitude. But ... in Central Europe the decrease of heat is 1.8 degrees for about every 534 feet of vertical elevation, it follows that a difference of elevation of about 267 feet corresponds to the difference of one degree of latitude.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these empirical conversions (0.9°F per 1° latitude; ~1.8°F per 534 ft altitude → ~267 ft ≈ 1° latitude equivalence) when comparing mountain climates to sea-level latitudinal positions in Central Europe; treat values as regional empirical rules, not universal constants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tropical Cordilleras lapse rate (empirical)
rubrics_metrics.description: In that part of the Cordilleras which falls within the tropics ... observations ... at an elevation of upward of 19,000 feet, gave a decrease of 1 degree for every 341 feet; and my friend Boussingault found, thirty years afterward, as a mean result, 319 feet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For tropical high mountains, use a lapse-rate approximation of ~1°F per 319–341 ft (empirical). Note that local factors (nocturnal radiation, plateaux effects) can alter this.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and distinction of the lower limit of perpetual snow
rubrics_metrics.description: The lower limit of perpetual snow ... is the lowest line at which snow continues during summer; it must be distinguished from three other phenomena, namely, the annual fluctuation of the snow-line, the occurrence of sporadic falls of snow, and the existence of glaciers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When defining or mapping the snow-line, explicitly separate (a) the lower limit of perennial snow, (b) seasonal fluctuations, (c) sporadic snow events, and (d) presence of glaciers—each has different causes and implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Controlling causes of snow-line elevation
rubrics_metrics.description: The phenomenon ... is extremely complicated, depending on the general relations of temperature and humidity, and on the form of the mountains. ... we shall find that the controlling causes are the differences in the temperature of different seasons of the year; the direction of the prevailing winds and their relations to land and sea; the degree of dryness or humidity in the upper strata of the air; the absolute thickness of the accumulated masses of fallen snow; the relation of the snow-line to the total height of the mountain; the relative position of the latter in the chain to which it belongs, and the steepness of its declivity; the vicinity of either summits likewise perpetually covered with snow; the expansion, position, and elevation of the plains from which the snow mountain rises ... whether it be covered with wood or waving grass; and whether, finally, it consist of a dry and rocky soil, or of a wet and marshy bottom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess all listed factors when analyzing regional snow-line elevation; do not attribute snow-line changes to latitude or mean annual temperature alone—topography, wind patterns, continental configuration, vegetation, and substrate all matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regional variability of snow-line (empirical examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: The snow-line ... rises or descends markedly between regions (examples: Cordilleras, Chile branch higher than equatorial Quito; Aconcagua sometimes free of snow due to evaporation in extremely dry air; in the Himalaya the snow-line higher on the northern declivity under the influence of the Tibetan highlands).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use local observational data (e.g., Pentland, Darwin, Darwin's Beagle notes, regional explorers) to characterize snow-line; expect significant inter-regional asymmetry (windward/leeward, continental plateau effects).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of August's psychrometer for hygrometric determinations
rubrics_metrics.description: Our knowledge of the hygrometric relations ... has been very materially augmented ... by the general application of August's psychrometer, framed in accordance with the views of Dalton and Daniell, for determining the relative quantity of vapor, or the condition of moisture of the atmosphere, by means of the difference of the 'dew point' and of the temperature of the air.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine relative humidity via psychrometric dew-point methods (dry and wet bulb difference) following Dalton/Daniell/August; compare readings across stations and heights to infer moisture distribution; cite observers (Boussingault, Gay-Lussac, Saussure) for historical calibration examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hygrometric observations and interpretation caveats
rubrics_metrics.description: Strata of air at Zurich and on the Faulhorn ... have raised doubts regarding the greater dryness of the mountain air which appeared to be proved by the hygrometric measurements ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat mountain hygrometric data with caution—local microclimates, instrument placement, and differing methods can produce conflicting inferences; compare multiple observers and instruments before generalizing about 'dryness' at altitude.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dove's formulation of vapor elasticity vs wind direction
rubrics_metrics.description: According to the exposition made by Dove ... it would appear that, in our northern zone, 'the elastic force of the vapor is greatest with a southwest, and least with a northeast wind. On the western side of the windrose this elasticity diminishes, while it increases on the eastern side; on the former side, for instance, the cold, dense, and dry current of air repels the warmer, lighter current containing an abundance of aqueous vapor, while on the eastern side it is the former current which is repulsed by the latter.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When interpreting vapor pressure and humidity patterns, account for prevailing wind direction and its interaction with continental/oceanic air masses (e.g., SW brings higher vapor elasticity in northern zones; NE brings lower).

rubrics_metrics.name: Vegetation/leaf water uptake as an explanation for verdure without rain
rubrics_metrics.description: The agreeable and fresh verdure ... in many trees in districts within the tropics, where, for five or seven months of the year, not a cloud is seen ... proves that the leaves are capable of extracting water from the atmosphere by a peculiar vital process of their own ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider foliar water uptake and micro-scale physiological processes as an explanation for plant vigor in arid but high-humidity/condensation environments (e.g., fog, dew), rather than assuming precipitation is the only water source.

rubrics_metrics.name: Atmospheric electricity empirical findings (electrometric observations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Limiting itself to results yielded by electrometric observations ... the physical description of the universe should merely notice the incontestable increase of intensity in the general positive electricity of the atmosphere accompanying an increase of altitude and the absence of trees, its daily variations ... and its variations in the different seasons of the year, at different distances from the equator, and in the different relations of continental or oceanic surface.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use electrometers (Colladon's apparatus, Saussure's electrometer with constraints) to document altitude, vegetation-cover, diurnal and seasonal patterns of atmospheric electric charge; note that instrument technique (e.g., fixed conductor) matters for valid comparison.

rubrics_metrics.name: Electric equilibrium: ocean vs land effects and island-induced storms
rubrics_metrics.description: The electric equilibrium is less frequently disturbed where the aerial ocean rests on a liquid base than where it impends over the land; and it is very striking to observe how, in extensive seas, small insular groups affect the condition of the atmosphere, and occasion the formation of storms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect more frequent electric disturbances over land than over open ocean; small islands and land-water contrasts can locally perturb atmospheric electricity and storm formation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cloud electrical charge by appearance (Peltier's experiments)
rubrics_metrics.description: Slate-gray clouds are charged, according to Peltier's experiments at Paris, with negative, and white, red, and orange-colored clouds with positive electricity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use cloud color/appearance as one (imperfect) empirical indicator of sign of cloud electric charge per Peltier; treat as observational rule-of-thumb subject to exceptions and dependent on local conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arago's classification of lightning types and temporal characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: According to Arago's investigations ... the evolution of light (lightning) is of three kinds -- zigzag, and sharply defined at the edges; in sheets of light, illuminating a whole cloud ...; and in the form of fire-balls.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish lightning events by morphology (zigzag strokes, sheet lightning, globular lightning); note durations: first two very brief (~1/1000 second), globular lightning can remain visible several seconds—implications for observation and instrumentation.
